publisher: Jianlin Su et al. · Zhuiyi Technology
title: How RoPE turns position into a rotation angle so attention sees only relative distance
summary: The RoFormer paper proposes Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE): instead of adding position vectors to tokens, it rotates queries and keys by a position-dependent angle, so only the position difference remains in the dot product. We work through the 2D rotation by hand, the speed table, and long-range decay, then separate the experimental claims that hold up from those that need a discount.
ai_summary: The RoFormer paper (Jianlin Su et al., Zhuiyi Technology, 2021) introduces RoPE: it treats each pair of dimensions in the query and key as a plane and rotates them by an angle determined by token position, so the dot product depends only on the relative position of two tokens. The paper derives this solution in the 2D case, gives multiple rotation frequencies from fast to slow with base 10000 and an elementwise implementation, proves that an upper bound on the dot product decays with distance, and shows RoPE can be combined with linear attention. Experiments include WMT14 English-German translation, BERT-style pretraining, GLUE, Performer, and Chinese long-text matching; the GLUE BERT baseline is taken from the original BERT paper's test set and is not fully comparable with this paper's validation-set results.
brief: Problem: Attention has no sense of word order; existing position encodings are all additive, and relative position encodings also require changing the expanded attention-score formula.
Method: Rotate queries and keys by position, with different speeds for each dimension pair; the dot product then contains only relative position.
Results: Pretraining converges faster, Chinese long-text models can read 1024 positions and do so more accurately; RoPE works directly with linear attention.
Limits: Small-scale experiments; GLUE ends three wins and three losses, and the baseline is not measured with the same ruler; the authors themselves cannot explain the faster convergence.

paper.title: RoFormer: Enhanced Transformer with Rotary Position Embedding
paper.authors: Jianlin Su, Yu Lu, Shengfeng Pan, Ahmed Murtadha, Bo Wen, Yunfeng Liu

cover.headline: Close reading: the original RoPE paper

nodes.label: Only n − m remains in the dot product

sections.h: The short version: what this paper actually does

blocks.p: In April 2021, Jianlin Su and five coauthors at Zhuiyi Technology in Shenzhen posted this paper on arXiv. The rotary position embedding (RoPE) it introduced later became one of the most common ways for open-source LLMs to tell a model where each token sits in a sequence; LLaMA, covered in another close reading on this site, uses it.

The problem comes from the Transformer itself: attention only sees "what is similar to what" and has no built-in sense of token order, so position information must be supplied separately. Earlier approaches were almost all additive: give each position a vector and add it to the token embedding, or add a distance-related term to the attention scores.

RoPE changes that to multiplication, and a special kind of multiplication: rotation. Treat each pair of dimensions in the query and key vectors as an arrow on a plane, and rotate the token at position m by m times a fixed angle. Since rotation does not change lengths, the dot product of two arrows depends only on the angle between them, so the attention score between position m and position n naturally depends only on the distance n − m: you encode absolute positions, but what you get is relative position.

The paper also proves two useful properties: the upper bound on the dot product shrinks as distance grows, and RoPE can be used directly with linear attention, which earlier relative position encodings could not do. The experiments are small in scale: translation, BERT-style pretraining, GLUE fine-tuning, Performer, and Chinese long-text matching.

callout.title: In one sentence
callout.text: Instead of adding a position vector to each token, rotate the query and key by an angle determined by position. The dot product of the two rotated vectors keeps only their position difference, so attention naturally looks only at relative distance.

callout.title: Three small concepts to get started
callout.text: Don't worry if they are new; these three are enough:
list: **Dot product**: multiply corresponding entries of two vectors and add them up. In 2D, that equals the product of the two arrows' lengths times the cosine of the angle between them: the more aligned they are, the larger it is.
**Query (q) and key (k) in attention**: each token produces a q and a k; the dot product of token m's q and token n's k determines how much m attends to n. See our Transformer close read for details.
**Rotation**: turn an arrow around the origin by an angle; its length stays the same, only the direction changes.

sections.h: Problem: how does a Transformer know word order?

blocks.p: Feed "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" to an attention layer with no position information, and it sees the same bag of words and computes the same result. Every Transformer therefore needs position encoded separately. The paper splits existing methods into two groups:

list: **Absolute position encoding**: give position i a vector p_{i} and add it to the token embedding before computing q, k, and v. The original Transformer generates p_{i} from sines and cosines; BERT and GPT treat it as trainable parameters. The downside is that the model learns "position 37", while what matters more in language is often "the word three positions back"; the trainable version also only learns up to a maximum length L.

**Relative position encoding**: split the attention score q_{m}^{⊺} k_{n} into four terms, then replace the position-dependent terms with something that depends only on distance m − n. Transformer-XL, DeBERTa, and T5 take this route, and T5 simply adds a learnable bias for each distance. The downside is that this modifies the expanded attention score and is tied tightly to the attention computation.

blocks.p: The paper points out that these methods all build on the idea of adding position into the representation. It asks the reverse question: can we find functions that encode position into q and k directly so their dot product automatically depends only on relative position? Written as a formula:

parts.desc: Functions that turn token x_{m} and its position m into query and key; these are what we need to solve for.
Dot product, the core of the attention score.
A function that sees only the tokens themselves and the position difference m − n: absolute positions m and n must not appear on their own.

formula.note: Section 3.4.1 solves this equation in the 2D case: the length must not change with position, and the angle must grow uniformly with position. The answer is rotation.

sections.h: Core idea: position is a rotation angle

blocks.p: Start with the simplest 2D case. q and k are both arrows on a plane. Rotate the query at position m by mθ and the key at position n by nθ, where θ is an angle chosen in advance:

parts.desc: As in standard attention, first project the token vector into a query.
A 2D rotation matrix: rotates the arrow counterclockwise by α without changing its length.
Rotating both vectors once is equivalent to rotating only k by the difference between their angles. The absolute positions m and n disappear; only n − m remains.

formula.note: In complex numbers this is cleaner: q_{m} = q · e^{imθ}, k_{n} = k · e^{inθ}, and the dot product is the real part of q · k^{*} · e^{i(m−n)θ}. That is equation (12) in the paper.

fig.title: Hand-worked check: same distance, same attention score
fig.subtitle: Illustrative 2D case: q = k = (1, 0), with each position rotated by θ = 30°. Dot product = cos((n − m) × 30°); computed here from equation (12) in the paper.
fig.note: Rows 2 and 3 have completely different positions but the same distance, so their dot products are the same. But the last row exposes the problem: with only one angle, distance 12 rotates all the way back around and becomes indistinguishable from distance 0. That is why real RoPE uses many different angles.

callout.title: Like a wall clock
callout.text: A clock with only a second hand comes back to the same place every minute, so it cannot tell 1 second from 61 seconds. Add the minute and hour hands, and the three together can distinguish long stretches of time. RoPE splits the vector into many pairs, each with a different rotation speed: fast ones distinguish nearby positions, slow ones distinguish distant ones.

sections.h: Scaling to higher dimensions: many dimension pairs, many speeds

blocks.p: If the vector is d-dimensional, with d even, split it into d/2 pairs of adjacent dimensions; each pair rotates in its own plane, and the i-th pair has speed θ_{i}:

parts.desc: A block-diagonal matrix: d/2 2×2 rotation blocks along the diagonal, where the i-th block rotates by mθ_{i}.
The angle, in radians, by which the i-th dimension pair rotates per position step. The first pair rotates 1 radian; later pairs are slower, with the slowest close to 1/10000.
The same base used by the original Transformer's sinusoidal position encoding.

formula.note: These rotation matrices are orthogonal, so they do not change vector length, which the paper says keeps position encoding stable. Note that RoPE rotates only q and k, not v; and it applies in the attention operation of every layer, not just added once at the input.

fig.title: Rotation speed, from fast to slow: positions per full turn for each dimension pair
fig.subtitle: Illustrative: d = 128, computed from θ_{i} in equation (15) of the paper; a full turn = 2π / θ_{i}, computed here.
fig.note: Like a clock: the fast dimension pairs are sensitive to nearby position differences, while the slow pairs change gradually and can distinguish very long distances. The last column is a rough heuristic, not a conclusion from the paper.

blocks.p: In practice, you do not need to actually multiply by a large matrix that is mostly 0s. Section 3.4.2 gives an elementwise version: two elementwise multiplications plus one addition are enough.

parts.desc: Swap each pair and negate the first number: that is exactly what a 90° rotation of a coordinate pair does.
Depends only on position m, so it can be precomputed and reused.

sections.h: Three properties: relative position, long-range decay, and linear-attention compatibility

blocks.p: **1. Built-in relative position.** We saw in the previous section that q and k each rotate by their own absolute position, leaving only the position difference in the dot product. Unlike earlier relative position encodings, RoPE does not modify the attention-score formula; it simply rotates q and k before taking the dot product.

**2. Long-range decay.** Section 3.4.3 proves that an upper bound on the q–k dot product shrinks as distance grows. The intuition: at position difference r, the i-th dimension pair's contribution is multiplied by a unit arrow rotated by rθ_{i}. At r = 0 all arrows point the same way; as r grows, arrows at different speeds point in scattered directions, so they cancel more when summed. The paper plots this decay with a single quantity (Figure 2), and we recomputed it from the paper's definition:

fig.title: The upper bound shrinks with distance
fig.subtitle: Illustrative: d = 128, computed from the quantity (1 / (d/2)) · Σ|S_{j}| in Section 3.4.3, where S_{j} is the sum of the first j unit arrows; numbers computed here.
fig.note: This is an upper bound, not the attention score itself: distant tokens can still get high scores, but the ceiling is lower. The paper sees this as matching the intuition that tokens far apart are usually less related.

blocks.p: **3. Works with linear attention.** Ordinary attention computes a score for every pair of tokens, so the cost grows quadratically with sequence length. Linear attention methods such as Performer first transform q and k separately with a non-negative function, then use the associativity of matrix multiplication to reduce the cost to linear in sequence length. Earlier relative position encodings modify each pair's score, which blocks that path. RoPE only rotates the transformed q and k individually, without pairing them up, so it can be used directly.

The trade-off is that, to avoid dividing by zero, the denominator is left in its unrotated form, while the numerator can contain negative terms, so the weights on the values are no longer strictly normalized probabilities that sum to 1. The paper concedes this and says the computation "can still model the importance of values."

callout.title: "RoPE is just a better position vector to add to the token embedding."
callout.text: No. RoPE has no position vector to add: it applies a position-dependent rotation to q and k inside every attention layer, while the token embeddings themselves and v carry no position. This is the fundamental difference from the original Transformer, BERT, and GPT: addition becomes multiplication.

sections.h: Experiments: small scale, so treat each conclusion separately

blocks.p: All the paper's experiments were run on two cloud servers, each with four V100 GPUs, far smaller than later LLM-scale work. The main results:

list: **Machine translation**: on WMT 2014 English-to-German, about 4.5 million sentence pairs, replacing the original Transformer-base position encoding with RoPE raised BLEU from 27.3 to 27.5. The paper reports only this one number, with no run-to-run variance.

**BERT-style pretraining**: replacing BERT's position encoding with RoPE, using batch size 64, maximum length 512, and 100k training steps, made the masked language modeling loss drop faster (Figure 3, left).
**Performer**: on Enwik8, adding RoPE to a 12-layer linear attention model made the loss fall faster and reach a lower value at the same number of steps (Figure 3, right).

blocks.p: **GLUE fine-tuning** is the part to read carefully. The paper says RoFormer "significantly outperforms" BERT on three of the six tasks:

fig.title: RoFormer vs. BERT: three wins, three losses, and mismatched metrics
fig.subtitle: From Table 2 of the paper. The BERT row matches the GLUE test-set scores in Table 1 of the original BERT paper exactly; the RoFormer row is, according to the paper, the best average on the validation set.
fig.note: RoFormer is higher on MRPC, STS-B, and QQP, and lower on SST-2, QNLI, and MNLI. The 15-point gap on QQP is the most striking, but since one side is a test set and the other a validation set, that gap cannot be credited to RoPE.

blocks.p: **Chinese long text** is the part the paper most wants to prove. The authors took their own WoBERT, replaced its absolute position encoding with RoPE, and trained on about 34GB of Chinese text in six stages, with different maximum lengths from 128 to 1536. They then tested on CAIL2019-SCM, a legal case matching dataset with 8,964 triples and documents mostly longer than 512 characters:

fig.title: Long text: RoFormer can read up to 1024 positions
fig.subtitle: From Table 5 of the paper; accuracy (%), higher is better. The number after each model name is the maximum input length.
fig.note: When all are truncated to 512, the three are nearly tied; RoFormer's advantage comes from reading longer inputs. Note that BERT and WoBERT use absolute position encodings learned only up to 512, so they cannot be directly compared with the 1024 version.

blocks.p: The paper ends by admitting two limitations: it cannot explain why RoPE converges faster than other position encodings, and it cannot explain why it performs better on long text, because long-range decay is also a property of other position encodings.

list: **Inconsistent subscript for θ**: Equation (15) writes θ_{i} = 10000^{−2(i−1)/d}, with i starting at 1; Sections 3.3 and 3.4.3 write θ_{i} = 10000^{−2i/d}. The two differ by an index shift, which does not affect the idea, but choose one when implementing.

**The GLUE comparison is not apples to apples**: The six BERT numbers in Table 2 match the GLUE test-set scores in the original BERT paper exactly, while this paper says it reports validation-set results. The paper does not say where its BERT row comes from, nor does it mention that RoFormer is lower on the other three tasks.

**The “1.5% improvement” does not match the table**: Section 4.5.4 says RoFormer-1024 improves over WoBERT by an absolute 1.5%, but in Table 5 the test-set gap is 1.69 (69.79 vs. 68.10) and the validation-set gap is 2.00 (66.07 vs. 64.07). The only exactly 1.5-point difference in the table is RoFormer-1024 versus its own 512-token version (69.79 vs. 68.29). Moreover, comparing 1024 with 512 already mixes in the benefit of being able to read longer inputs.

**Sign of the position difference**: Equation (11) writes g(x_{m}, x_{n}, m − n), while Equation (21) in the derivation writes n − m. The two are just different conventions, but a paper should keep them consistent.
**A subscript typo**: Equation (32) writes q = f_{q}(x_{m}, 0) = W_{q} x_{n}; the right-hand side should be x_{m}.
**A typo in the Table 2 title**: it says “GLEU” instead of GLUE.

sections.h: Afterward: the most common position encoding in open-source LLMs

list: **LLaMA and later open-source models**: The LLaMA paper states that it removes absolute position encoding and adds RoPE in every layer of the network. Many later open-source models have followed suit.

**Extending context length**: RoPE's rotation speeds are determined by the base 10000. Later work found that by “compressing” positions into the range the model was trained on, or by adjusting the rotation speeds of different dimensions, the length a model can read can be extended several times over. This has become a common technique for long-context models.

**Small implementation differences**: The paper pairs adjacent dimensions; many popular implementations instead pair each dimension in the first half with the corresponding dimension in the second half. This only reorders the dimensions and is mathematically equivalent, but when using someone else's weights you must match the pairing.

**Connection to this line of work**: T5 uses relative position in the form of one learnable bias per distance; RoPE gets the same relative-position behavior from rotation without changing the attention-score formula.

blocks.p: Next, we return to the attention computation itself: **FlashAttention**. It does not change the result of attention; instead, it reorders the GPU memory reads and writes so that attention on long sequences is faster and uses much less memory.

sections.h: Test yourself: did you get it?

quiz.q: How does RoPE make attention scores depend only on relative position?
options: Learn a separate bias for each distance and add it to the score.
Rotate q at position m by mθ and k at position n by nθ; in the dot product the two rotations cancel into a single rotation that depends only on n − m.
Add a position vector to each token vector.
Mask out tokens that are too far apart.
quiz.why: Rotation does not change length, and the dot product of two rotated vectors depends only on the difference between their angles. So the absolute positions m and n cancel out, leaving only n − m.

quiz.q: Why does RoPE use different rotation speeds for different dimension pairs?
options: With a single speed, after one full turn the vector is back where it started, so near and far become indistinguishable; fast and slow speeds together are what let the model tell near and far apart at once.
To make the vector length smaller.
To stay compatible with BERT's weights.
quiz.why: Just as a clock with only a second hand cannot tell 1 second from 61 seconds, the fast dimension pairs distinguish nearby position differences and the slow pairs distinguish distant ones.

quiz.q: In Table 2, RoFormer beats BERT 86.4 to 71.2 on QQP. Why can't we treat that as a big win for RoPE?
options: Because QQP is not a GLUE task.
Because the BERT row comes from the original paper's test set, while the RoFormer row comes from the validation set; the two are not measured with the same ruler.
Because QQP is only about long text.
quiz.why: The BERT row matches the original BERT paper's GLUE test-set scores exactly, while this paper reports validation-set results. Scores for the same task can differ a lot between the two sets.

blocks.p: After reading this, you should be able to answer the following questions:

list: Why does a Transformer need position encoding? What are the shortcomings of absolute and relative position encodings?
What exactly does RoPE's “rotation” rotate? Why does only relative position remain in the dot product?
What does θ_{i} = 10000^{−2(i−1)/d} mean? Why are both fast and slow speeds needed?
What is long-range decay, and why is it only an upper bound?
Why can RoPE be combined with linear attention while earlier relative position encodings cannot?
Among the paper's experiments, which conclusions are reliable and which should be discounted?
